claim: The prevalence of implantable devices (orthopedic, cardiac, neuromodulation) increases in the population as does the pervasiveness of conditions requiring MRI studies for diagnosis (musculoskeletal diseases, infections, or cancer).
source: One limitation on the ability to monitor health in older adults using magnetic resonance (MR) imaging is the presence of implants, where the prevalence of implantable devices (orthopedic, cardiac, neuromodulation) increases in the population, as does the pervasiveness of conditions requiring MRI studies for diagnosis (musculoskeletal diseases, infections, or cancer).
evidence: This is a general statement about population trends without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: The in silico VHP-Female model corresponds to a 60-year-old female with a body mass index of 36.
source: The in silico VHP-Female model (250 parts with an additional 40 components specifically characterizing embedded implants and resultant surrounding tissues) corresponds to a 60-year-old female with a body mass index of 36.
evidence: Direct description of the model characteristics.

claim: The testbed has been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a medical device development tool for 1.5 T orthopedic implant examinations.
source: The testbed has very recently been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a medical device development tool for 1.5 T orthopedic implant examinations.
evidence: Statement of regulatory approval status.

claim: In 2020, 26% of the US population over 65 was estimated to carry a large joint or spinal implant.
source: In 2020, 26% of the US population over 65 was estimated to carry a large joint or spinal implant (Kanal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanal et al., 2015.

claim: 12.6 million patients over 65 who carry orthopedic or cardiac implants will need an MR study within 10 years, according to an estimate in 2020.
source: Simultaneously, 12.6 million patients over 65 who carry orthopedic or cardiac implants will need an MR study within 10 years, according to an estimate in 2020 (Kanal et al., 2015) with this number expected to rise.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanal et al., 2015.

claim: Over 70% of the estimated 3 million pacemakers in the US are implanted in patients older than 65.
source: Similarly, over 70% of the estimated 3 million pacemakers in the US are implanted in patients older than 65 (Lim et al., 2019; Puette et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lim et al., 2019 and Puette et al., 2022.

claim: Approximately 20% of pacemaker patients will need an MR study within 12 months of device implantation.
source: where approximately 20% of these patients will need an MR study within 12 months of device implantation (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: MR safe items are nonconducting, nonmetallic, and nonmagnetic items, such as a plastic Petri dish.
source: MR safe items are nonconducting, nonmetallic, and nonmagnetic items, such as a plastic Petri dish (Shellock et al., 2009).
evidence: Definition supported by citation to Shellock et al., 2009.

claim: MR unsafe items include ferromagnetic materials and should not enter the MR scanner room.
source: MR unsafe items include in particular ferromagnetic materials (Shellock et al., 2009); they should not enter the MR scanner room (US Food and Drug Administration, 2023a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shellock et al., 2009 and US Food and Drug Administration, 2023a.

claim: All devices that contain any metallic components, such as titanium (regardless of ferromagnetism), are MR conditional and will need to be evaluated and labeled for RF-induced heating, image artifact, force, and torque.
source: All other devices that contain any metallic components, such as titanium (regardless of ferromagnetism), are MR conditional and will need to be evaluated and labeled for radio frequency (RF)-induced heating, image artifact, force, and torque (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021.

claim: The number of cleared US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) submissions for orthopedic implantable devices with MR labeling has been growing exponentially since 2014, approaching 100 in 2019.
source: Given the large numbers of implants subject to conditional labeling, the number of cleared US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) submissions for orthopedic implantable devices with MR labeling has been growing exponentially since 2014 (Fujimoto et al., 2020), approaching 100 in 2019 (Fujimoto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fujimoto et al., 2020.

claim: Practical testing is limited by constraints related to cost and resources, including testing tools.
source: However, practical testing is limited by constraints related to cost and resources, including testing tools (Fujimoto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujimoto et al., 2020.

claim: A number of implants have been labeled 'MR Not Evaluated', which precludes patients' access to MR imaging procedures.
source: As a result, a number of implants have been labeled 'MR Not Evaluated', which precludes patients' access to MR imaging procedures (Fujimoto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujimoto et al., 2020.

claim: Other implants may be labeled too restrictively, limiting patient access to MR imaging.
source: Other implants may be labeled too restrictively (Kanal et al., 2015), limiting patient access to MR imaging (US Food and Drug Administration, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kanal et al., 2015 and US Food and Drug Administration, 2022.

claim: Up to 2 million elderly patients in the US are potentially affected by MR labeling uncertainty.
source: When estimating combined data from Kanal et al., 2015; Fujimoto et al., 2020; US Food and Drug Administration, 2022; US Food and Drug Administration, 2023b, up to 2 million elderly patients in the US are potentially affected by MR labeling uncertainty.
evidence: Estimate based on combined data from multiple cited sources.

claim: The most important consequence of MR labeling uncertainty is restricting general access to MR imaging studies for patients with implants.
source: Presumably, the most important consequence of this uncertainty is restricting general access to MR imaging studies for patients with implants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of labeling issues.

claim: Periprosthetic joint infection following total hip replacement surgery occurs in only 1–2% of primary arthroplasties.
source: A prime example of the latter is periprosthetic joint infection following total hip replacement surgery, which occurs in only 1–2% of primary arthroplasties (Fischbacher and Borens, 2019; Zanetti, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischbacher and Borens, 2019 and Zanetti, 2020.

claim: Periprosthetic joint infection occurs in up to 30% of revision arthroplasties.
source: but in up to 30% of revision arthroplasties (Zanetti, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanetti, 2020.

claim: Periprosthetic joint infection occurs due to mechanical loosening and dislocation, currently the most common causes for revision of total hip arthroplasty in the US.
source: This form of infection occurs due to mechanical loosening and dislocation, currently the most common causes for revision of total hip arthroplasty in the US (Li and Glassman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Glassman, 2018.

claim: Periprosthetic joint infection-related mortality is approaching 5–8% at 1 year.
source: Periprosthetic joint infection-related mortality is approaching 5–8% at 1 year (Fischbacher and Borens, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischbacher and Borens, 2019.

claim: Results of MR imaging with metal artifact reduction were recently shown to be the most accurate tool in the diagnosis of several biomarkers of periprosthetic hip joint infection.
source: but results of MR imaging with metal artifact reduction were recently shown to be the most accurate tool in the diagnosis of several biomarkers of periprosthetic hip joint infection (Zanetti, 2020; Galley et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zanetti, 2020 and Galley et al., 2020.

claim: One major safety concern relevant to both passive and active implants is implant heating within MR RF and gradient coils.
source: One major safety concern, relevant to both passive and active implants, is implant heating within MR RF and gradient coils (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021; Song et al., 2018; Al-Dayeh et al., 2020; Winter et al., 2021; Wooldridge et al., 2021; Arduino et al., 2021; Arduino et al., 2022a; Bassen and Zaidi, 2022; Arduino et al., 2022b; Clementi et al., 2022; Oberle, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Numerical simulations with virtual human models generate accurate predictions of temperature rise accepted by the FDA.
source: Along with the required yet not entirely anatomical ASTM phantom test and other similar phantom tests (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021; Song et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2021; Wooldridge et al., 2021; Bassen and Zaidi, 2022; Arduino et al., 2022b), numerical simulations with virtual human models generate accurate predictions of temperature rise (Al-Dayeh et al., 2020; Winter et al., 2021; Wooldridge et al., 2021; Arduino et al., 2022a; Clementi et al., 2022; Oberle, 2021) accepted by the FDA (Oberle, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including FDA acceptance.

claim: The electromagnetic and thermal simulation algorithms based on finite element, finite difference, and boundary element methods are reasonably well developed.
source: The electromagnetic and thermal simulation algorithms based on finite element, finite difference, and boundary element methods are reasonably well developed (Makarov et al., 2017; Noetscher et al., 2023; Noetscher et al., 2021; Noetscher, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple sources.

claim: Accessible, full body, detailed anatomical virtual human models reflecting major age, sex, race, and obesity variations are severely lacking.
source: However, accessible, full body, detailed anatomical virtual human models reflecting major age, sex, race, and obesity variations are severely lacking.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: Creation of virtual human models is a long, tedious, and labor-intensive process requiring manual and semiautomatic supervised segmentation of full body MR images, surface mesh reconstruction, mesh intersection resolution, software compatibility and robustness testing, and examination of hundreds of different body compartments by anatomical experts.
source: Their creation is a long, tedious, and labor-intensive process. Even today, it requires manual and semiautomatic supervised segmentation of full body MR images, surface mesh reconstruction, mesh intersection resolution, software compatibility and robustness testing, and finally examination of hundreds of different body compartments by anatomical experts.
evidence: Description of the process based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The Virtual Population is an excellent collection of in silico human body models intended for MR safety assessment.
source: An excellent collection of in silico human body models intended for this purpose is the Virtual Population, a product of the IT'IS Foundation (Oberle, 2021; Gosselin et al., 2014) widely used in both industrial and academic applications.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oberle, 2021 and Gosselin et al., 2014.

claim: The Virtual Population is relatively homogeneous, consisting of reasonably fit, younger Caucasian European subjects, representing a comparatively limited subsection of human anatomy and physiology.
source: While this population has many highly detailed body models, it is relatively homogeneous: reasonably fit, younger Caucasian European subjects, representing a comparatively limited subsection of human anatomy and physiology.
evidence: This is an assessment of the Virtual Population characteristics.

claim: Three obese models were added to the Virtual Population in 2023, with two of the three not truly anatomical and obtained via morphing (the 'Fats' model being the exception).
source: Although three obese models were added in 2023 (IT'IS Foundation, 2023), two of the three are not truly anatomical and were obtained via morphing (the 'Fats' model being the exception).
evidence: Supported by citation to IT'IS Foundation, 2023.

claim: No background MRI data enabling independent tissue structure verification have been made publicly available for the Virtual Population set.
source: Also, while models are available for purchase and for research purposes, no background MRI data enabling independent tissue structure verification have been made publicly available for this population set.
evidence: Statement about data availability.

claim: The in silico VHP-Female model has 250 anatomical structures with an additional 40 components specifically modeling embedded implants.
source: The in silico VHP-Female model (250 anatomical structures with an additional 40 components specifically modeling embedded implants Noetscher et al., 2021) characterizes a 60-year-old female subject with a body mass index of 36.
evidence: Description of the model with citation to Noetscher et al., 2021.

claim: The open-source version of the VHP-Female model has over 600 registered users from both industry and academia worldwide.
source: The open-source version of this model (NEVA Electromagnetics, LLC, 2015) has over 600 registered users from both industry and academia worldwide.
evidence: Statement about user base with citation.

claim: The testbed includes the in silico model, an implant embedding procedure, a generic parameterizable MR RF birdcage two-port coil model, a workflow for computing heat sources on the implant surface and neighboring tissues, and a thermal FEM solver directly linked to the MR coil simulator.
source: The testbed includes the in silico model, an implant embedding procedure, a generic parameterizable MR RF birdcage two-port coil model, a workflow for computing heat sources on the implant surface and neighboring tissues, and a thermal FEM solver directly linked to the MR coil simulator to estimate implant heating based on an MR imaging protocol.
evidence: Description of testbed components.

claim: The primary target of the testbed is MR labeling of large orthopedic implants.
source: The primary target is MR labeling of large orthopedic implants.
evidence: Statement of the testbed's primary purpose.

claim: The testbed has recently been approved by the FDA as a medical device development tool for 1.5 T orthopedic implant examinations.
source: The testbed has recently been approved by the FDA as a medical device development tool (Neva Electromagnetics, LLC, 2022) for 1.5 T orthopedic implant examinations.
evidence: Statement of FDA approval with citation.

claim: The implant registration enforces an anatomically correct implant position and requires a certain part of the bone matter (cortical and/or trabecular) to be removed as necessary.
source: The implant registration enforces an anatomically correct implant position, and a certain part of the bone matter (cortical and/or trabecular) to be removed as necessary.
evidence: Description of the implant registration procedure.

claim: A semiautomatic implant registration algorithm requiring limited user intervention has been employed based on using at least two anchor nodes per implant: a fixed node and a floating node.
source: A semiautomatic implant registration algorithm requiring limited user intervention has been employed based on the principal idea to use at least two anchor nodes per implant: a fixed node and a floating node.
evidence: Description of the algorithm methodology.

claim: A generic, parameterized, and tunable MR RF birdcage two-port coil model at 64 MHz (1.5 T) with a variable number of rungs was implemented in Ansys Electronics Desktop.
source: A generic, parameterized, and tunable MR RF birdcage two-port coil model (high-, low-, or bandpass), at 64 MHz (1.5 T) with a variable number of rungs was implemented in Ansys Electronics Desktop (Ansys HFSS, Figure 2a).
evidence: Description of the coil model with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The coil model is used to compute heat sources – either specific absorption rate (SAR) in W/kg or power loss density in W/m3 at any point in the body, including on the surface of the implants.
source: This model is used to compute heat sources – either specific absorption rate (SAR) in W/kg or power loss density in W/m3 at any point in the body, including on the surface of the implants (Figure 2b, c; Kozlov et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of model functionality with reference to figures and citation.

claim: An Ansys FEM transient thermal solver was employed to determine tissue temperature rise close to the implant caused by the heat sources.
source: An Ansys FEM transient thermal solver was employed to determine tissue temperature rise close to the implant caused by the heat sources.
evidence: Description of the thermal solver used.

claim: The thermal solver requires knowing the relevant thermal properties of the tissues.
source: It requires knowing the relevant thermal properties of the tissues.
evidence: Statement about solver requirements.

claim: The thermal solver may approximately model blood perfusion, which is less important for bone, but is important for cardiac implants and other soft tissue implants.
source: The solver may approximately model blood perfusion, which is less important for bone, but is important for cardiac implants and other soft tissue implants (Winter et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about solver capabilities with citation.

claim: The entire testbed has been integrated into Ansys Workbench, which allows the combination of different multiphysics modules within a single environment.
source: The entire testbed has been integrated into Ansys Workbench, which allows the combination of different multiphysics modules within a single environment, as shown in Figure 3.
evidence: Description of software integration with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The output of the electromagnetic solver is the input to the thermal solver.
source: In this way, the output of the electromagnetic solver (Figure 3A and B) is the input to the thermal solver (Figure 3D).
evidence: Description of workflow with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Both accurate FEM solvers utilize the same human model geometry throughout, but with different material properties (thermal vs electromagnetic).
source: Both accurate FEM solvers utilize the same human model geometry throughout, but with different material properties (thermal vs electromagnetic).
evidence: Description of solver implementation.

claim: Devices are to be labeled for a 1 hr MR session, including both scan and rest times, according to the FDA's guidance document.
source: This is described in the FDA's guidance document (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021) (cf. also examples in Shellock et al., 2009) where devices are to be labeled for a 1 hr MR session, including both scan and rest times.
evidence: Supported by citations to FDA guidance and Shellock et al., 2009.

claim: The FDA guidance states a certain interleaving combination of scan and rest times that guarantees implant heating is less than 5°C or another specified number.
source: The guidance states a certain interleaving combination of scan (e.g., 5 min) and rest (e.g., 15 min) times that guarantees implant heating is less than 5°C or another specified number (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to FDA guidance.

claim: The FDA-required procedure is a measurement test in an ASTM gel-based homogeneous phantom.
source: The FDA-required procedure is a measurement test in an ASTM gel-based homogeneous phantom (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to FDA guidance and Song et al., 2018.

claim: When performing relevant numerical modeling, the pulse sequences and scan times should be converted to equivalent CW (continuous wave) operation, which is easier to model.
source: When performing relevant numerical modeling, the pulse sequences and scan times should be converted to equivalent CW (continuous wave) operation, which is easier to model.
evidence: Statement about modeling methodology.

claim: The response of the ASTM phantom is quite different from that of a real body, which includes bones and other tissues of varying electrical and thermal conductivities, as well as blood circulation and perfusion.
source: However, the response of the ASTM phantom is quite different from that of a real body, which includes bones and other tissues of varying electrical and thermal conductivities, as well as blood circulation and perfusion.
evidence: Statement about phantom limitations based on knowledge.

claim: In several test cases, the testbed prototype predicted a higher maximum temperature rise (up to 40% higher) at the implant tips versus in vitro experiments with a simplified gel phantom.
source: In several test cases, our testbed prototype predicted a higher maximum temperature rise (up to 40% higher) at the implant tips versus in vitro experiments with a simplified gel phantom.
evidence: Comparison of testbed predictions with experimental results.

claim: In other cases, and for other implants, the heating was substantially lower (by 50% or so) compared to phantom experiments.
source: In other cases, and for other implants, however, the heating was substantially lower (by 50% or so).
evidence: Comparison of testbed predictions with experimental results.

claim: The in silico testbed will augment the ASTM measurements with accurate multiphysics modeling.
source: Therefore, the in silico testbed will augment the ASTM measurements with accurate multiphysics modeling.
evidence: Statement about the intended use of the testbed.

claim: The multiphysics modeling can assist with implant design in an efficient manner.
source: Additionally, this modeling can assist with implant design in an efficient manner.
evidence: Statement about potential application.

claim: This work is solely focused on the RF safety aspects of MR labeling.
source: We note that this work is solely focused on the RF safety aspects of MR labeling.
evidence: Statement about scope of work.

claim: The results expressed in this work should be considered supplemental to existing published guidelines.
source: The results expressed herein should be considered supplemental to existing published guidelines.
evidence: Statement about how results should be interpreted.

claim: For a long titanium femoral nail subject to three cycles of 15 min with a 2.3 W/kg average equivalent SAR exposure followed by 5 min of rest in a 1.5 T MRI coil, the model predicts that the temperature near the implant reaches 41°C after the first exposure with its final value approaching 45°C, a total increase of about 10°C.
source: Figure 4 shows an example of testing results for a long titanium femoral nail subject to three cycles of 15 min with a 2.3 W/kg average equivalent SAR exposure followed by 5 min of rest, resulting in a 1 hr total exposure in a 1.5 T MRI coil. The model predicts that the temperature near the implant reaches 41°C after the first exposure with its final value approaching 45°C, a total increase of about 10°C which is clearly unacceptable!
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Further simulations show that 4 min exposures followed by 16 min of rest would be a safe solution for the long titanium femoral nail.
source: Further simulations show that 4 min exposures followed by 16 min of rest would be a safe solution.
evidence: Results from additional simulations.

claim: In the testbed, the exposure time is arbitrary and can be rapidly tested and adjusted (within 5–7 min) to meet the FDA requirements and construct the proper MR exposure protocol.
source: In the testbed, the exposure time is arbitrary and can be rapidly tested and adjusted (within 5–7 min) to meet the FDA requirements (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021) and construct the proper MR exposure protocol.
evidence: Description of testbed capabilities with citation.

claim: The most challenging and important cases correspond to testing large and potentially resonant metal implants with relatively sharp tips or terminations since detecting resonance requires accurate high-frequency modeling.
source: The most challenging and important cases correspond to testing large and potentially resonant metal implants (Song et al., 2018) with relatively sharp tips or terminations since detecting resonance requires accurate high-frequency modeling.
evidence: Statement about challenging cases with citation.

claim: In Hue et al., 2018, a simulated percutaneous RF ablation surgical procedure using MR heating was performed in ex vivo bovine liver in a 1.5 T scanner.
source: One extreme example was studied in Hue et al., 2018, where a simulated percutaneous RF ablation surgical procedure using MR heating was performed in ex vivo bovine liver in a 1.5 T scanner.
evidence: Description of experiment from cited study.

claim: The device under study in Hue et al., 2018 was a bent long wire 'antenna' made resonant at the scanner Larmor frequency with an adjustable series capacitor, terminated in a simulated RF ablation needle (a 15 cm long 16 AWG/1.30 mm diameter bare copper wire), the tip of which was embedded into the liver.
source: The device under study was a bent long wire 'antenna' made resonant at the scanner Larmor frequency with an adjustable series capacitor. The antenna, a 26 AWG (0.40 mm) Teflon-insulated silver-plated copper wire taped around the edge of the patient table, was terminated in a simulated RF ablation needle (a 15 cm long 16 AWG/1.30 mm diameter bare copper wire), the tip of which was embedded into the liver to simulate the percutaneous ablation of a solid hepatic tumor.
evidence: Description of experimental setup from cited study.

claim: The peak tissue temperature increase imaged in Hue et al., 2018 by the proton resonance frequency shift method was 20°C.
source: The peak tissue temperature increase imaged in Hue et al., 2018, by the proton resonance frequency shift method (20°C)
evidence: Experimental result from cited study.

claim: A 22°C increase was recorded by a fiber optic temperature sensor at the needle tip in Hue et al., 2018.
source: and a 22°C increase recorded by a fiber optic temperature sensor at the needle tip
evidence: Experimental result from cited study.

claim: The modeling testbed predicted a 23°C increase for the ablation needle experiment, which agreed well with the experimental measurements of 20°C and 22°C from Hue et al., 2018.
source: The peak tissue temperature increase imaged in Hue et al., 2018, by the proton resonance frequency shift method (20°C) and a 22°C increase recorded by a fiber optic temperature sensor at the needle tip agreed well with our modeled prediction of a 23°C increase using the modeling testbed.
evidence: Comparison of testbed prediction with experimental results.

claim: A very fine FEM mesh resolution is required to accurately resolve temperature rise close to a sharp lead tip with a diameter of 1.3 mm.
source: A very fine FEM mesh resolution is required to accurately resolve temperature rise close to a sharp lead tip with a diameter of 1.3 mm – Figure 5.
evidence: Statement about modeling requirements with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Local automated adaptive FEM mesh refinement is achieved in the testbed, which is a unique property of the present testbed.
source: This is achieved using local automated adaptive FEM mesh refinement, which is a unique property of the present testbed.
evidence: Description of testbed capability.

claim: The temperature rise in the surrounding tissues of a large orthopedic metallic implant subject to MR imaging is a significant point of concern and a potential barrier for the development of better implants.
source: The temperature rise in the surrounding tissues of a large orthopedic metallic implant subject to MR imaging is a significant point of concern and a potential barrier for the development of better implants.
evidence: Statement about the problem being addressed.

claim: Numerical electromagnetic and thermal modeling offers a way to solve the complex problem of implant heating with a sufficient degree of accuracy.
source: Numerical electromagnetic and thermal modeling offers a way to solve this complex problem with a sufficient degree of accuracy.
evidence: Statement about the solution approach.

claim: A complete testbed for realistic implant modeling was developed, which includes a detailed FEM-compatible obese human female model, a parameterized tunable generic MR coil model, a method for implant embedding, and an accurate RF solver directly coupled with a transient thermal solver.
source: We developed a complete testbed for realistic implant modeling, which includes a detailed FEM-compatible obese human female model, a parameterized tunable generic MR coil model, a method for implant embedding, and an accurate RF solver directly coupled with a transient thermal solver.
evidence: Summary of what was developed.

claim: In the testbed, the MR exposure time is arbitrary and can be readily adjusted and rapidly tested (typically within ~5–7 min) to meet regulatory requirements and construct a proper MR exposure protocol.
source: In the testbed, the MR exposure time is arbitrary and can be readily adjusted and rapidly tested (typically within ~5–7 min). This enables the user to meet regulatory requirements (US Department of Health and Human Services et al., 2021) and to construct a proper MR exposure protocol.
evidence: Description of testbed capabilities with citation.

claim: A cross-platform compatibility of the in silico model has been established previously.
source: A cross-platform compatibility of the in silico model has been established previously (Yanamadala et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yanamadala et al., 2016.

claim: Further validation of cross-platform electromagnetic and thermal coupling performance is currently underway with Dassault Systèmes CST Studio Suite software package.
source: Further validation of cross-platform electromagnetic and thermal coupling performance is currently underway with Dassault Systèmes CST Studio Suite software package.
evidence: Statement about ongoing work.

claim: The testbed along with the open-source version of the human model VHP-Female College is available online at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.2jm63xswt.
source: The testbed along with the open-source version of the human model VHP-Female College (NEVA Electromagnetics, LLC, 2015) is available online at https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.2jm63xswt.
evidence: Statement about data availability with citation.

claim: The VHP-Female model is based on the Visible Human Project cryo-section dataset.
source: (1) an in silico human model based on the widely available Visible Human Project (VHP) cryo-section dataset
evidence: The model name VHP-Female indicates it is based on the Visible Human Project dataset.

claim: The testbed uses Ansys Electronics Desktop/Mechanical as the FEM modeling software workbench.
source: (2) a finite element method (FEM) modeling software workbench from Ansys (Electronics Desktop/Mechanical) to model MR radio frequency (RF) coils and the temperature rise modeling in heterogeneous media.
evidence: Direct statement about the software used.
